claim: Crenactin is a filament-forming protein from the crenarchaeon Pyrobaculum calidifontis.
source: The similarity of eukaryotic actin to crenactin, a filament-forming protein from the crenarchaeon Pyrobaculum calidifontis supports the theory of a common origin of Crenarchaea and Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about crenactin.

claim: The similarity of eukaryotic actin to crenactin supports the theory of a common origin of Crenarchaea and Eukaryotes.
source: The similarity of eukaryotic actin to crenactin, a filament-forming protein from the crenarchaeon Pyrobaculum calidifontis supports the theory of a common origin of Crenarchaea and Eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on structural similarities.

claim: Monomeric structures of crenactin and actin are similar.
source: Monomeric structures of crenactin and actin are similar, although their filament architectures were suggested to be different.
evidence: This refers to previously established structural knowledge.

claim: Crenactin filament architectures were previously suggested to be different from actin.
source: Monomeric structures of crenactin and actin are similar, although their filament architectures were suggested to be different.
evidence: This refers to prior literature suggesting differences.

claim: Crenactin forms bona fide double helical filaments.
source: Here we report that crenactin forms bona fide double helical filaments that show exceptional similarity to eukaryotic F-actin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Crenactin double helical filaments show exceptional similarity to eukaryotic F-actin.
source: Here we report that crenactin forms bona fide double helical filaments that show exceptional similarity to eukaryotic F-actin.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on structural comparison.

claim: The structure of the crenactin filament was solved to 3.8 Å resolution using cryo-electron microscopy and helical reconstruction.
source: With cryo-electron microscopy and helical reconstruction we solved the structure of the crenactin filament to 3.8 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by experimental data.

claim: The 'hydrophobic plug' loop in crenactin rearranges when forming double filaments.
source: When forming double filaments, the 'hydrophobic plug' loop in crenactin rearranges.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryoEM data.

claim: Arcadin-2 is encoded by the arcade gene cluster.
source: Arcadin-2, also encoded by the arcade gene cluster, binds tightly with its C-terminus to the hydrophobic groove of crenactin.
evidence: This is based on genomic information.

claim: Arcadin-2 binds tightly with its C-terminus to the hydrophobic groove of crenactin.
source: Arcadin-2, also encoded by the arcade gene cluster, binds tightly with its C-terminus to the hydrophobic groove of crenactin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: Arcadin-2 binding is reminiscent of eukaryotic actin modulators such as cofilin and thymosin β4.
source: Binding is reminiscent of eukaryotic actin modulators such as cofilin and thymosin β4 and arcadin-2 is a depolymeriser of crenactin filaments.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis based on structural similarity.

claim: Arcadin-2 is a depolymeriser of crenactin filaments.
source: Binding is reminiscent of eukaryotic actin modulators such as cofilin and thymosin β4 and arcadin-2 is a depolymeriser of crenactin filaments.
evidence: This is a functional finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The work further supports the theory of shared ancestry of Eukaryotes and Crenarchaea.
source: Our work further supports the theory of shared ancestry of Eukaryotes and Crenarchaea.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Eukaryotic actin and non-eukaryotic actin-like proteins and their filaments fulfil diverse functions.
source: Eukaryotic actin and non-eukaryotic actin-like proteins and their filaments fulfil diverse functions, from cellular motility and plasticity, cellular junctions, cytokinesis and phagocytosis in eukaryotic cells to cell shape maintenance, intracellular organisation and plasmid segregation in bacteria and archaea (Pilhofer and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: All actins and actin-like proteins share a well-conserved three-dimensional structure at the subunit level.
source: At the subunit level, all actins and actin-like proteins share a well-conserved three-dimensional structure as well as the longitudinal protofilament contact architecture that facilitates linear polymerisation into strands (protofilaments) and polymerisation-induced ATPase activation (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Ozyamak et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All actins and actin-like proteins share the longitudinal protofilament contact architecture that facilitates linear polymerisation into strands.
source: At the subunit level, all actins and actin-like proteins share a well-conserved three-dimensional structure as well as the longitudinal protofilament contact architecture that facilitates linear polymerisation into strands (protofilaments) and polymerisation-induced ATPase activation (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Ozyamak et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Actin forms right-handed, parallel and staggered filaments in all Eukaryotes (F-actin).
source: While actin forms right-handed, parallel and staggered filaments in all Eukaryotes (F-actin) (Holmes et al., 1990; von der Ecken et al., 2015), actin-like proteins differ in their filament architectures
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MamK forms right-handed filaments that have juxtaposed, non-staggered subunits.
source: MamK, required for magnetosome alignment in magnetotactic bacteria, forms right-handed filaments that have juxtaposed, non-staggered subunits (Bergeron et al., 2016; Löwe et al., 2016; Ozyamak et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MamK is required for magnetosome alignment in magnetotactic bacteria.
source: MamK, required for magnetosome alignment in magnetotactic bacteria, forms right-handed filaments that have juxtaposed, non-staggered subunits (Bergeron et al., 2016; Löwe et al., 2016; Ozyamak et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ParM produces left-handed, staggered filaments.
source: ParM, making mitosis-like bipolar spindles during E. coli R1 plasmid segregation, produces left-handed, staggered filaments (Bharat et al., 2015; Gayathri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ParM makes mitosis-like bipolar spindles during E. coli R1 plasmid segregation.
source: ParM, making mitosis-like bipolar spindles during E. coli R1 plasmid segregation, produces left-handed, staggered filaments (Bharat et al., 2015; Gayathri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MreB forms apolar, non-staggered and non-helical filaments that bind directly to membranes.
source: MreB, essential for cell-shape maintenance in most rod-shaped bacteria, forms the most divergent filaments when compared to F-actin, as it forms apolar, non-staggered and non-helical filaments that bind directly to membranes (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MreB is essential for cell-shape maintenance in most rod-shaped bacteria.
source: MreB, essential for cell-shape maintenance in most rod-shaped bacteria, forms the most divergent filaments when compared to F-actin, as it forms apolar, non-staggered and non-helical filaments that bind directly to membranes (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Crenactin is found in certain organisms of the order Thermoproteales within the phylum Crenarchaeota.
source: Attempts to trace back the origins of today's eukaryotic F-actin filaments led to the discovery of crenactin found in certain organisms of the order Thermoproteales within the phylum Crenarchaeota (Crenarchaea, part of the 'TACK' superphylum) (Ettema et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Crenarchaea is part of the 'TACK' superphylum.
source: Attempts to trace back the origins of today's eukaryotic F-actin filaments led to the discovery of crenactin found in certain organisms of the order Thermoproteales within the phylum Crenarchaeota (Crenarchaea, part of the 'TACK' superphylum) (Ettema et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Organisms of the TACK superphylum show unique similarities to Eukaryotes in cytokinesis.
source: Together with other findings that report unique similarities between organisms of the TACK superphylum and Eukaryotes in cytokinesis (Lindås et al., 2008; Samson et al., 2008), membrane remodelling, cell shape determination and protein recycling, this has led to a theory of a common origin with eukaryotic cells (Guy and Ettema, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Crenactin filaments share a common ancestor with F-actin.
source: Hence, it has been proposed that crenactin filaments share a common ancestor with F-actin.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on evolutionary inference.

claim: In Pyrobaculum calidifontis, crenactin is encoded within the arcade cluster of genes, together with four arcadins.
source: In Pyrobaculum calidifontis, crenactin is encoded within the arcade cluster of genes, together with four arcadins, and has been proposed to be part of a cell-shape maintenance system (Ettema et al., 2011).
evidence: This is genomic information supported by citation.

claim: Crenactin has been proposed to be part of a cell-shape maintenance system.
source: In Pyrobaculum calidifontis, crenactin is encoded within the arcade cluster of genes, together with four arcadins, and has been proposed to be part of a cell-shape maintenance system (Ettema et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Arcadin-4 is related by sequence to SMC-like proteins, in particular Rad50.
source: Not much is known about the arcadins, but arcadin-4 is related by sequence to SMC-like proteins, in particular Rad50 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Previous crenactin structures showed crenactin to be single-stranded.
source: All previous crenactin structures (two crystal-structures, PDB IDs 4CJ7, 4BQL, and one cryoEM reconstruction) (Braun et al., 2015; Izoré et al., 2014; Lindås et al., 2014) showed crenactin to be single-stranded
evidence: This refers to prior structural studies.

claim: It was proposed that the position of the hydrophobic plug was incompatible with the formation of an F-actin-like double-stranded helix because of steric hindrance.
source: it was proposed that the position of the hydrophobic plug was incompatible with the formation of an F-actin-like double-stranded helix because of steric hindrance (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis from cited work.

claim: A dramatic rearrangement of the hydrophobic plug was observed, moving it upwards by as much as 21 Å.
source: In our filament structure presented here, we observed a dramatic rearrangement of the hydrophobic plug, moving it upwards, towards subdomain IB, by as much as 21 Å (Figure 2B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryoEM data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the new position, the hydrophobic plug interacts extensively with subunits of the opposite strand.
source: In this new position, the loop interacts extensively with subunits of the opposite strand (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), essentially the same function as the hydrophobic plug has in F-actin.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Most of the lateral interactions in crenactin are of hydrophilic nature.
source: As in F-actin, most of these lateral interactions are of hydrophilic nature in contrast to its name (von der Ecken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a structural observation with comparison to F-actin.

claim: A hydrophilic interaction between subdomain IIB on one strand and subdomain IA on the opposite strand helps to keep the double filament architecture stable.
source: In addition to the hydrophobic plug, a hydrophilic interaction between subdomain IIB on one strand and subdomain IA on the opposite strand helps to keep the double filament architecture stable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Single-stranded filaments imaged in previous studies were possibly enabled by the high-salt concentrations used.
source: Based on the mostly hydrophilic nature of the inter-strand interactions, we believe it is possible that the single-stranded filaments imaged in previous studies were enabled by the high-salt concentrations used (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the nature of interactions.

claim: Crenactin subunits within the same strand are held together via three main areas of interactions.
source: For longitudinal assembly, crenactin subunits within the same strand are held together via three main areas of interactions (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in figures.

claim: The D-loop is located within subdomain IB and is folded into a small alpha helix.
source: Particularly significant is the well-conserved D-loop (DNase I binding loop) located within subdomain IB. Folded into a small alpha helix, it interacts with the previous subunit via a surface usually referred to as the 'hydrophobic groove' in actin (Dominguez, 2004).
evidence: This is a structural observation with reference to actin nomenclature.

claim: The longitudinal and lateral interactions between neighbouring subunits are similar to an unprecedented extent between crenactin and F-actin.
source: Although the size of the hydrophobic plug is unique to crenactin, the longitudinal and lateral interactions between neighbouring subunits are similar to an unprecedented extent between crenactin and F-actin.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis.

claim: The similarity in actin and crenactin helical parameters is striking, with only a difference of ~2 Å in rise and ~4.5° in twist.
source: The similarity in actin and crenactin helical parameters is striking, with only a difference of ~2 Å in rise and ~4.5° in twist (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ATPase active site is highly conserved between crenactin and actin with key residues in the same place in both structures.
source: Furthermore, the ATPase active site is also highly conserved with key residues, such as the nucleophilic water activator Q164 (Q137 in actin) (Iwasa et al., 2008), in the same place in both structures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 2D with citation.

claim: ATP binding and polymerisation induce inter-domain angle conformational changes in actins and actin-like proteins.
source: As has been reported for many actins and actin-like proteins (Fujii et al., 2010; Gayathri et al., 2012; van den Ent et al., 2014), ATP binding, and more importantly polymerisation, induce inter-domain angle conformational changes, closing the groove between domains IB and IIB and removing a propeller twist of domains I and II against each other upon polymerisation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: This conformational change was also observed for crenactin.
source: We also observed this change for crenactin.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the data.

claim: The rotation flattens the molecule in the polymer, removing the propeller twist between domains I and II.
source: The rotation flattens the molecule in the polymer, removing the propeller twist between domains I and II (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in supplementary figure.

claim: This motion is conserved in both eukaryotic actin and its prokaryotic homologues MreB and ParM.
source: This motion is conserved in both eukaryotic actin (Fujii et al., 2010; von der Ecken et al., 2015) and its prokaryotic homologues MreB (van den Ent et al., 2014) and ParM (Gayathri et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: This conformational change is most likely a pre-requisite of ATPase switching upon longitudinal polymerisation for the entire actin-like protein family.
source: and is most likely a pre-requisite of ATPase switching upon longitudinal polymerisation for the entire actin-like protein family.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations across the protein family.

claim: A sequence alignment of several arcadin-2s revealed that a small conserved C-terminal domain is separated from the core of the protein by a non-conserved, presumably unstructured linker.
source: A sequence alignment of several arcadin-2s revealed that a small conserved C-terminal domain is separated from the core of the protein by a non-conserved, presumably unstructured linker (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Addition of ATP to crenactin resulted in an increase of scattering, most likely because of the formation of filaments.
source: Addition of ATP to crenactin resulted in an increase of scattering, most likely because of the formation of filaments (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with interpretation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Subsequent addition of arcadin-2 resulted in rapid depolymerisation of the polymers as scattering diminished.
source: Subsequent addition of arcadin-2 resulted in rapid depolymerisation of the polymers as scattering diminished.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from light scattering.

claim: Addition of a C-terminally truncated version of arcadin-2 had no effect on crenactin polymerisation.
source: Addition of a C-terminally truncated version of arcadin-2 had no effect, suggesting that the conserved C-terminal α-helix of arcadin-2 was responsible for the depolymerisation of crenactin filaments.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from light scattering.

claim: The conserved C-terminal α-helix of arcadin-2 is responsible for the depolymerisation of crenactin filaments.
source: Addition of a C-terminally truncated version of arcadin-2 had no effect, suggesting that the conserved C-terminal α-helix of arcadin-2 was responsible for the depolymerisation of crenactin filaments.
evidence: This is an inference from the truncation experiment.

claim: A peptide spanning the last 17 amino acids of arcadin-2 (187–203) triggered depolymerisation of the filaments at a similar rate as full-length arcadin-2.
source: To test this, we performed the same experiment using a peptide spanning the last 17 amino acids of arcadin-2 (187–203). Indeed, the peptide triggered depolymerisation of the filaments at a similar rate as full-length arcadin-2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Crenactin becomes monomeric upon addition of the C-terminal arcadin-2 peptide.
source: This effect was confirmed by analytical ultra centrifugation, showing that crenactin becomes monomeric upon addition of the C-terminal arcadin-2 peptide (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from analytical ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Crenactin polymerisation is controlled by arcadin-2.
source: We conclude that crenactin polymerisation is controlled by arcadin-2 and that arcadin-2's C-terminal helix is essential for this activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Arcadin-2's C-terminal helix is essential for controlling crenactin polymerisation.
source: We conclude that crenactin polymerisation is controlled by arcadin-2 and that arcadin-2's C-terminal helix is essential for this activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Co-expression and subsequent purification of crenactin and arcadin-2 resulted in a tight 1:1 complex.
source: Co-expression and subsequent purification of crenactin and arcadin-2 resulted in a tight 1:1 complex (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The dissociation constant of the crenactin:arcadin-2 complex is 31 ± 4 nM (n = 4).
source: The dissociation constant of this complex was very low with a Kd of 31 ± 4 nM (n = 4), as measured by SPR (Surface Plasmon Resonance, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SPR shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The crystal structure of crenactin in complex with arcadin-2 C-terminal peptide was solved to 1.6 Å by X-ray crystallography.
source: The structure was solved to 1.6 Å by X-ray crystallography (Table 1) providing detailed insights into crenactin, binding to ATP and, more importantly, showing how arcadin-2 induced depolymerisation of the filaments.
evidence: This is a methodological statement with data in Table 1.

claim: The arcadin-2 peptide is located in the hydrophobic groove on crenactin.
source: The arcadin-2 peptide was located in the hydrophobic groove on crenactin, a cavity formed between subdomains IA and IIA (Figure 3D) (Dominguez, 2004).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the filament, the hydrophobic groove is occupied by the D-loop of the following subunit in a strand, forming one half of the longitudinal contact.
source: In the filament, this hydrophobic groove is occupied by the D-loop of the following subunit in a strand, forming one half of the longitudinal contact (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The nanomolar interaction between arcadin-2 peptide and the hydrophobic pocket is likely due to a tryptophan and other hydrophobic residues.
source: The nanomolar interaction between arcadin-2 peptide and the hydrophobic pocket is likely due to a tryptophan and other hydrophobic residues, making strong contacts as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Arcadin-2 C-terminal residues form the only interacting domain with crenactin.
source: Additional SPR experiments showed that arcadin-2 C-terminal residues formed the only interacting domain with crenactin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from SPR shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Arcadin-2 disrupts crenactin filaments by competing with the D-loop for the hydrophobic groove.
source: Given the high affinity of arcadin-2 for crenactin we propose that arcadin-2 disrupts crenactin filaments by competing with the D-loop for the hydrophobic groove.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: Many eukaryotic actin-interacting proteins use the hydrophobic groove as a binding site.
source: Many of the plethora of eukaryotic actin-interacting proteins use the same hydrophobic groove as arcadin-2 on crenactin as a binding site, such as ADF/cofilin (Paavilainen et al., 2008), gelsolin (McLaughlin et al., 1993), thymosin β4 (Irobi et al., 2004), ciboulot (Hertzog et al., 2004) and the Wiskott–Aldrich Syndrome protein WH2 domain (WASP) (Chereau et al., 2005), amongst others (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The hydrophobic groove has been termed a 'hot spot' for actin-binding proteins.
source: It has therefore been termed a 'hot spot' for actin-binding proteins and there is also one such case in bacteria, the ParM:ParR interaction that involves binding of the ParR adaptor protein in ParM's hydrophobic groove (Figure 3F) (Gayathri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established nomenclature with citation.

claim: The ParM:ParR interaction involves binding of the ParR adaptor protein in ParM's hydrophobic groove.
source: It has therefore been termed a 'hot spot' for actin-binding proteins and there is also one such case in bacteria, the ParM:ParR interaction that involves binding of the ParR adaptor protein in ParM's hydrophobic groove (Figure 3F) (Gayathri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The high affinity of arcadin-2 and its strong bulk depolymerisation activity makes it a possible functional homologue of actin sequesters such as thymosin β4.
source: Proteins binding to the hydrophobic groove of actin facilitate a variety of functions depending on additional interactions and their affinity, but it seems to us that the high affinity of arcadin-2 and its strong bulk depolymerisation activity makes it a possible functional homologue of actin sequesters such as thymosin β4.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on functional similarity.

claim: The finding that arcadin-2 inhibits crenactin polymerisation in a manner similar to known actin sequesters provides further evidence for the parallel evolution of crenactin and eukaryotic actin.
source: Our finding that arcadin-2 inhibits crenactin polymerisation in a manner similar to known actin sequesters provides further evidence for the parallel evolution of crenactin and eukaryotic actin since they have both maintained the function of the hydrophobic groove (Bernander et al., 2011; Guy and Ettema, 2011).
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on functional similarity.

claim: Crenactin and eukaryotic actin have both maintained the function of the hydrophobic groove.
source: Our finding that arcadin-2 inhibits crenactin polymerisation in a manner similar to known actin sequesters provides further evidence for the parallel evolution of crenactin and eukaryotic actin since they have both maintained the function of the hydrophobic groove (Bernander et al., 2011; Guy and Ettema, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparative functional observation.

claim: There is a lack of any detectable sequence similarity between arcadin-2 and actin sequesters.
source: Because of a lack of any detectable sequence similarity between arcadin-2 and actin sequesters, arcadin-2's mode of action might have arisen by convergent evolution.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Arcadin-2's mode of action might have arisen by convergent evolution.
source: Because of a lack of any detectable sequence similarity between arcadin-2 and actin sequesters, arcadin-2's mode of action might have arisen by convergent evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation.

claim: The arcade cluster encodes three more proteins: arcadin-1, -3 and -4.
source: The arcade cluster encodes three more proteins: arcadin-1, -3 and -4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is genomic information shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The crystal structure of arcadin-1 shows it is not related to any known eukaryotic actin binding proteins.
source: Our crystal structure of arcadin-1 shows it not to be related to any known eukaryotic actin binding proteins (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Arcadin-1 does not show obvious similarity to any other protein currently in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
source: and also does not show obvious similarity to any other protein currently in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
evidence: This is based on structural database searches.

claim: Arcadin-1 forms tight dimers in the crystals.
source: Arcadin-1 forms tight dimers in the crystals (Figure 4B) and also oligomers (Figure 4C and D), with octamers being likely.
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Arcadin-1 forms oligomers, with octamers being likely.
source: Arcadin-1 forms tight dimers in the crystals (Figure 4B) and also oligomers (Figure 4C and D), with octamers being likely.
evidence: This is based on analytical ultracentrifugation shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Arcadin-1 interacts moderately with crenactin with a Kd of 15 ± 3 µM.
source: A surface plasmon resonance assay revealed that arcadin-1 interacts moderately with crenactin (Kd of 15 ± 3 µM, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from SPR shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Arcadin-1 did not affect crenactin polymerisation as monitored by light scattering and EM.
source: However, arcadin-1 did not affect crenactin polymerisation as monitored by light scattering and EM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from light scattering and EM.

claim: The double helical filament structure of crenactin corrects previous reports of single crenactin strands.
source: Our double helical filament structure of the crenarchaeal actin-like protein crenactin corrects previous reports of single crenactin strands (Braun et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the new structural data contradicting prior work.

claim: The double helical filament structure firmly re-affirms the idea that Crenarchaea and eukaryotic cells share a common ancestor.
source: and firmly re-affirms the idea that Crenarchaea and eukaryotic cells share a common ancestor (Guy and Ettema, 2011).
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on structural similarity.

claim: The arcade cluster contains similarities to today's actin cytoskeleton as exemplified by arcadin-2's ability to depolymerise crenactin through interaction with the hydrophobic groove.
source: This is further supported by our finding that the arcade cluster contains other similarities to today's actin cytoskeleton as exemplified by arcadin-2's ability to depolymerise crenactin through interaction with the hydrophobic groove (Dominguez, 2004), most likely sequestering monomers with high affinity - a mode of action utilised by several eukaryotic actin modulators.
evidence: This is a comparative functional interpretation.

claim: Arcadin-2 most likely sequesters monomers with high affinity.
source: This is further supported by our finding that the arcade cluster contains other similarities to today's actin cytoskeleton as exemplified by arcadin-2's ability to depolymerise crenactin through interaction with the hydrophobic groove (Dominguez, 2004), most likely sequestering monomers with high affinity - a mode of action utilised by several eukaryotic actin modulators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high affinity binding and depolymerization activity.

claim: The recent discovery by metagenomics of Lokiarchaeota shows it is monophyletic with Eukaryotes.
source: The recent discovery by metagenomics of Lokiarchaeota (Spang et al., 2015), being monophyletic with Eukaryotes, has unearthed actin homologues that are much closer to eukaryotic actin as judged by sequence identity than crenactin
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited metagenomic study.

claim: Lokiarchaeota has actin homologues that are much closer to eukaryotic actin as judged by sequence identity than crenactin.
source: The recent discovery by metagenomics of Lokiarchaeota (Spang et al., 2015), being monophyletic with Eukaryotes, has unearthed actin homologues that are much closer to eukaryotic actin as judged by sequence identity than crenactin
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis from cited work.

claim: Primordial crenactin already provided an excellent template for the evolution and the origin of the eukaryotic actin cytoskeleton.
source: although it is clear from our work that primordial crenactin already provided an excellent template for the evolution and the origin of the eukaryotic actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation based on the structural and functional similarities found.

claim: Crenactin forms right-handed, double-stranded, staggered filaments with a rise of 25.6 Å and a twist of 198.1°.
source: Crenactin forms right-handed, double-stranded, staggered filaments with a rise of 25.6 Å (half a subunits' length, hence staggered) between subunits and a twist of 198.1° (1-start, rotating between the two strands, equivalent to -161.9°) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a structural determination from cryoEM shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Eukaryotic F-actin filament has a rise of 27.5 Å and a twist of 193.6° (equivalent to −166.4°).
source: These values are very similar to the parameters of the eukaryotic F-actin filament, with a rise of 27.5 Å and a twist of 193.6° (equivalent to −166.4°, Figure 2A, Video 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (von der Ecken et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited work.

claim: Architecture and helical parameters make crenactin the closest F-actin homologue of any other actin-like filament investigated to date.
source: Architecture and helical parameters further add to the previously reported similarities in sequence and subunit structure (Ettema et al., 2011; Izoré et al., 2014; Lindås et al., 2014), making crenactin the closest F-actin homologue of any other actin-like filament investigated to date.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: Both reconstructions (double-stranded and single-stranded initial models) generated very similar double-helical density maps.
source: We found that both reconstructions generated very similar double-helical density maps, the one with lower symmetry at slightly lower resolution, as would be expected (3.8 Å vs 4.2 Å) because of the smaller number of asymmetric units averaged (Figure 1C), thus unequivocally demonstrating the double-stranded nature of the crenactin filaments.
evidence: This is an experimental result from cryoEM reconstruction shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The similarity of crenactin monomer to eukaryotic actin was unprecedented, with an overall RMSD of 1.6 Å, despite sequence identity of only ~20%.
source: The similarity of the monomer to eukaryotic actin was unprecedented, with an overall RMSD of 1.6 Å, despite sequence identity of only ~20%.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison from prior work.

claim: The hydrophobic plug is longer in crenactin but is inserted in the same part of the fold as in actin.
source: The hydrophobic plug is longer in crenactin but is inserted in the same part of the fold as in actin.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from prior work.

claim: Previous studies on the architecture of crenactin filaments were performed under high salt concentrations (>0.5 M KCl).
